# Overview

## Package Origins

Since we are working in Posit Cloud, we will need to set up our R
environment so that all of the libraries we need are installed and ready
to use.

Please note that Posit Cloud projects are independent, so you must
install packages **once per project**. If you are working on your local
machine, this does not apply, and a package installed in one project
will be available in another.

Throughout this course, we will use packages primarily from two sources:

1)  [CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive
    Network)](https://cran.r-project.org/): This is the central
    repository for R packages. Packages included in this repository can
    complete a wide variety of tasks to fit your scripting needs.
2)  [Bioconductor](https://www.bioconductor.org/): This is a repository
    that contains packages that are more focused on bioinformatic tasks.
    We will access more specialized packages well suited to course needs
    through this resource.

We will also install packages from GitHub. This is most commonly done
when you are working with packages still in development. While this adds
an installation step, it allows you to access novel and helpful code.

## Tips on Using Packages

-   To load a particular installed package into your environment, use
    the `library()` function.
    -   Example syntax: `library(tidyverse)` would load the `tidyverse`
        package into your workspace.
-   If you want to access a function without using the `library()`
    command, you can use the syntax `package_name::function_name()`
    -   Example: `jsonlite::flatten()` would run the `flatten` function
        *without* needing to load `jsonlite` first.
    -   This can also be extremely helpful if you install multiple
        packages that contain functions with identical names.
-   If you have a question about a particular function, you can run
    `?function_name` in the **console**, and the documentation will
    appear in the **Help** window.

# Installations

```{r note_t0}

## here, we record the start time prior to install
t0 <- Sys.time()

```

## CRAN Packages

We begin by installing all of the CRAN packages necessary for course
content.

**NOTE:** `tidyverse` is a large package that contains many other
packages, all of which focus on data cleaning and manipulation.
Consequently, while we don't explicitly install them, by installing
`tidyverse`, we gain access to many additional packages that will be
discussed throughout this course, including `tidyr`, `dplyr`, and
`ggplot2`.

```{r cran_install}

## identify all of the packages we need to get from CRAN
all_cran_pkgs <- c("knitr", "rmarkdown", "BiocManager", "utils", "rvest",
                   "janitor", "here", "tidyverse", "jsonlite", "data.table", 
                   "duckdb", "CDMConnector", "renv", "arrow", "patchwork", 
                   "devtools", "remotes")
  
## run install
install.packages(all_cran_pkgs)

```

## Bioconductor Packages

From there, we move to installing Bioconductor packages.

**NOTE:** Installing Bioconductor packages requires using the
`BiocManager::install()` function, making the installation syntax
slightly different from the chunk above.

```{r bioc_install}

all_bioc_pkgs <- c("metabolomicsWorkbenchR", "HMP16SData", "phyloseq")

BiocManager::install(all_bioc_pkgs,
                     update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)

```

## GitHub Packages

For this course, we will be using the following GitHub packages:

-   `microshades`: this package is designed to create data
    visualizations that are accessible for people with color vision
    deficiency

Because GitHub packages are coming from an external source, we have to
use the `remotes` package for access.

### Microshades

```{r gh_install_micro}

remotes::install_github("KarstensLab/microshades", dependencies = TRUE)

```

# Summarize Time Taken

Now that all of our installations have completed, we can look at how
long it took for them to complete.

```{r install_time}

tE <- Sys.time()

## print the duration of the install 
tE - t0

```

# Session Info

To confirm that all of the packages have successfully installed, we can
run `sessionInfo`. In addition to listing the packages themselves, it
will also show which versions you are using.

```{r inf}

sessionInfo()

```
